speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: asked the Prime Minister in light of CPIB’s findings on former Minister S Iswaran (a) whether the current system of checks and balances, including the governance of senior public officials and whistle-blowing processes, adequately deliver on its intended purposes; and (b) whether there are areas for further improvements or enhancements.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: In view of Mr S Iswaran’s case, some members of the public and various Members in this House, including Mr Edward Chia, Mr Derrick Goh, Ms Joan Pereira, Mr Darryl David and Mr Mohd Fahmi, have asked about our rules – whether they are adequate and should they be reviewed.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: And Mr Speaker, Sir, my response will also cover the matter raised in the questions by Mr Darryl David1 and Mr Mohd Fahmi2 which are scheduled for a subsequent Sitting.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I would invite Members to seek clarifications, if need be.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If the questions have been addressed, it may not be necessary for members to proceed with the Parliamentary Questions for future Sittings.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Our rules are meant to facilitate our work and keep our officers safe from being compromised.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: They should not be so onerous that our officers cannot operate.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Neither should they be so lax as to erode discipline and trust in our system.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: When an incident happens, we should not have a knee-jerk reaction and immediately tighten or add more rules.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, was it a case where the rules were clear, but were flouted or ignored?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If so, then what we need to do is not to adjust the rules, but to take action against the offender.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Second, was it a case where the rules were unclear?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If so, then we should clarify or simplify the rules.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But we should be mindful that not every grey area can be clarified, and for some matters, judgement may be required.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Our officers should not just understand the letter of the rule, but also the spirit.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Third, was it a case where the rules were too lax, or was it a new situation not envisaged or covered by the rules?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Maintaining the integrity of our system is a multi-pronged and continuous effort.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: At the individual level, we must have the right ethos and values; understand both the spirit and letter of the rules; and uphold them.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: At the team or organisation-level, we must look out for one another to minimise the chances of us being compromised, subverted, or succumbing to human frailties.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: At the system level, we must have regular internal audits, external audits and have institutions like Auditor-General's Office (AGO) and the Corrupt Practices Investigation Bureau (CPIB) to respond to issues not picked up by other layers of checks.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Hence, when incidents happen, we respond decisively and transparently to restore trust and confidence in our system.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is what we have done and what we will continue to do.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, Mr Edward Chia and Mr Derrick Goh asked about gifts.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Officers must never ask for gifts or favours, especially when they are in a position to influence or affect any decision involving the other party.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: An officer must not accept any gift offered to him, on account of his official position or his official work.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Our first instinct must be to decline any unsolicited gifts and return them, if possible.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If it is not possible or impractical to do so, we declare and account for it according to established processes.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is to ensure transparency and to maintain our probity.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If the officer wants to keep the gift, he may be allowed to do so if he pays for it after having its value assessed.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But should an officer accept multiple gifts of $49 repeatedly?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I think we know the answer from the spirit of the rule.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If such a pattern of behaviour is observed, it must stop.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We appreciate that it may not be practical to assess the value of the meal in the moment.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Officers must have good sense to know when they are being cultivated and reject such attempts.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: When in doubt, officers should inform their supervisors.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This does not mean that our officers should not go out and interact with non-Government stakeholders to understand the business and social communities.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It is part of our work to understand the world in order to govern responsively and responsibly.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As a practical measure to protect ourselves, I always advise our officers to avoid attending such events alone where the risk of being compromised is harder to manage.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: On the Code of Conduct for public officers, we review the rules annually to ensure that it remains relevant to the contexts we are facing and are going to face.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For each review, we will gather feedback and will consult stakeholders, including the unions.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If there are changes, they will be communicated to our officers.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Ms Joan Pereira and Mr Darryl David asked about the Code of Conduct for Ministers and Political Office Holders.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The last major changes were made in 2005 and included clarifications on the rules on acceptance of gifts, declarations of investments and directorships, amongst others.
Political Office Holders are also expected to abide by the Rules of Prudence, issued by the Prime Minister after every General Election to all People's Action Party (PAP) Members of Parliament.
Mr Edward Chia, Ms Joan Pereira and Mr Mohd Fahmi asked about the whistle-blowing process.
There are confidentiality and "non-retaliation" provisions in place to protect those who have reported in good faith.
We should let the law take its course and not jump to conclusions nor make statements that may prejudice the case or prematurely adjudge the processes that may have gone right or wrong.
This case is one that was picked up by CPIB and investigations were initiated without external pressure or interference.

In updating our rules, sharpening our implementation, and inculcating the right ethos and values to our officers, the Public Service and the Government will continue to draw lessons from this and other cases, whether local or overseas.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Given that business and cultural norms actually differ between countries and evolved.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, for example, in some cases, declining invitations to dinners or events may be perceived as disrespectful.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What are the standard operating procedures (SOPs) and training provided to public officers who advance trade relations and attract foreign direct investments (FDIs) and how often are these training materials updated?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, on the training of our public officers and second part about the difference between the Government and the private sector.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Our Public Service has a system of ensuring the Code of Conduct is known and observed.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We focus not just on the rules, as I have explained, but also the principles behind the rules.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The key principles are articulated in the Instruction Manuals with illustrative examples to help officers understand the rules.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is the process of how we inculcate the right values and ethos in our officers to help them understand not just the letter of the rule but the spirit behind the rule.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The context for public agencies is different from that of private companies.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Our Public Service is in the business of governance and providing public services to a nation of people from diverse backgrounds and who have different expectations and aspirations.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is very different from the private sector where they are more concerned with transactions between private parties.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For the public sector, we need to earn the respect and trust of the public and to put in place a fair system that it is not just about who you are and whether you can pay to access public services in a fair and transparent manner.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is why the Public Service hold ourselves to high standards of conduct to give confidence to all stakeholders that they will be treated fairly and transparently.
